# Matched control receipt for the NAX K-loop prefetch experiment

## 0. What this submission is

**This is a deliberate control, not an attempt to improve the score.** It is a
byte-exact restoration of three files to the current experiment base
(`747d130b`), submitted so that a candidate receipt dispatched from the same
session has a matched reference row. Its expected outcome is "no change versus
the current frontier". Please read it as the denominator of a paired
measurement rather than as a proposed optimization.

The paired candidate is submission `26b8e82a-9158-4fe1-83d5-fcf71a301e7e`,
which enables a depth-1 software pipeline in the routed NVFP4 gather-GEMM
kernel `fp_gather_qmm_rhs_expert_nax`. This control has that pipeline absent
entirely — the template parameter, the host lever, and the loader split are all
removed, because the files are restored to their base revision rather than
merely being toggled off.

## 1. Why a control receipt is needed at all

Published speedups are ratios against a same-session baseline, and the baseline
prefill draw is the noisy term: it swings about ±1.93 % run to run, while the
candidate's own run-to-run standard deviation is only 0.260 %. Reading a small
kernel-level effect off the published speedup therefore imports the baseline's
variance into the estimate and can easily hide or manufacture a 1–2 ms effect.

The discipline I use instead is to read every ledger row off the **raw**
`officialMetrics` of the candidate side, and to convert to milliseconds with a
fixed transformation:

```
S = 512000 * prefill_seconds_per_token          (prefill critical path, ms)
T = 1000 * decode_seconds_per_token - S/128     (marginal decode step, ms)
```

The `- S/128` term is not a convention. The decode measurement window contains
a full 512-token seed prefill: the clock starts before the seed is fed, and the
reported figure is the total divided by 128 steps. So

```
decode_seconds_per_token = (512/128) * prefill_seconds_per_token + T
```

I verified this identity exactly against a published receipt
(`4 * 0.00019120068359375 + 0.004143569335937499 = 0.0049083720703125`), and
the resulting speedups reproduce that receipt's published composite score to
full precision. Without subtracting the seed term, any prefill change leaks
into the apparent decode number and both axes become uninterpretable.

Having a control row measured in the same session, on the same host, under the
same thermal gate, lets me difference `S` directly and quote an effect in
milliseconds with a known noise floor (σ(S) = 0.318 ms, so the paired
difference has σ ≈ 0.4497 ms and a 3σ threshold of 1.35 ms).

## 2. Environment and how this control was produced

The submission archive is built from the working tree on disk over the
benchmark manifest's editable path list. I therefore produced this control by
checking the three experiment-touched files out of the base revision:

```
git checkout 747d130be532383d3eabd190f54f8b1b2bc6f9fd -- \
  Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/fp_quantized_nax.h \
  Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx-generated/fp_quantized_nax.cpp \
  Vendor/mlx-swift/Source/Cmlx/mlx/mlx/backend/metal/quantized.cpp
mlxfast submit --model senpai --note-file <this file>
git checkout HEAD -- <the same three paths>
```

Every other editable file is identical to the candidate submission, so the
difference between the two archives is exactly the mechanism under test.

## 3. Prior work this control serves

An earlier round measured four bit-exact in-kernel perturbations of this same
gather-GEMM against a matched control, each deliberately multiplying one
resource axis. The marginal window attributable to the kernel is
`W = 43.2619 ms`:

| arm | perturbation | ΔS | % of W | σ |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| M2 | double MMA + integer ALU | +2.046 ms | 4.7 % | 4.5σ |
| B2 | two extra threadgroup barriers | +0.841 ms | 1.9 % | 1.9σ |
| S3 | extra staging, **zero** extra DRAM bytes | +7.853 ms | 18.2 % | 17.5σ |
| S2 | extra staging, +5.89 GB of DRAM traffic | +15.961 ms | 36.9 % | 35σ |

That rules out a compute-bound explanation and rules out joint saturation, and
positively identifies the device→threadgroup staging path as the bottleneck,
split roughly 49 % load-issue and 51 % DRAM bytes. The pure-issue component is
6.887 ms — 15.9 % of the window — paid merely for *issuing* loads, independent
of bytes moved. That is the term the paired candidate attacks.

Those four numbers were themselves obtained with exactly this control
methodology, which is why I am willing to spend a receipt on the denominator
again rather than differencing against a stale row from an earlier session.

## 4. Sizing, so the control's value is legible

I rebuilt the staged-byte accounting for this kernel chunk by chunk from the
checkpoint and the shipped route histogram, because the carried campaign figure
was an analytic all-slots number. Three corrections emerged:

1. The shipped 512-token prefill dispatches this kernel **38** times, not 39.
   Layer 0 is dense and layer 39 diverts to an M=1 GEMV shortcut taken when the
   sequence is longer than one token and the mask is causal.
2. The carried byte total is **16.1 % too high**: it assumed all 256 expert
   slots on all 39 layers. Chunk-accurate accounting gives 8,379 chunks and
   **14.8264 GB** staged, versus a carried 17.66 GB. 20.26 % of expert slots
   receive zero rows and never construct a loader.
3. The M axis is padded twice at two granularities — staging and barriers at
   `BM = 64`, the MMA chain at `SM = 16` — so byte waste and FLOP waste are
   different quantities, which independently retires a "67 % of bandwidth and
   67 % of compute" ridge identity the corpus carried.

At 14.8264 GB over 43.2619 ms the kernel runs at 342.7 GB/s, 55.8 % of the
614 GB/s streaming ceiling. The pure streaming floor for those bytes is
24.15 ms, leaving **19.11 ms of headroom inside the window**. Because a
millisecond removed from prefill is paid on both scored axes (the prefill axis
directly, and the decode axis through the amortized seed prefill), the
elasticity is 0.374750 % of score per millisecond, so that headroom is worth
about 7.16 % of score — roughly 14× the 3σ detection threshold. Resolving
whether a pipeline reaches any of it is worth a clean denominator.

## 5. Expected result and how it will be read

I expect this receipt to land close to the current frontier and to be
`rejected` for not beating it. That is the intended outcome; a `rejected`
verdict here carries no information about correctness, and I will read
correctness, error, and the two floor verdicts separately from ranking status.

What I will extract is the raw `prefill_seconds_per_token` and
`decode_seconds_per_token`, convert to `S` and `T` by the formulae in §1, and
difference `S` against the candidate row. The pre-registered decision rule is:
if the candidate shows `ΔS ≥ −1.35 ms` the mechanism is declared a null, I stop
after these two receipts, and I write up a clean negative rather than spending
the third on a variant of a mechanism that did not move.

## 6. Caveats

Two receipts taken minutes apart on the same host under the same thermal gate
are not literally a same-session paired draw, so a slow thermal drift between
them would appear as a spurious ΔS. The 3σ threshold of 1.35 ms is set from
measured session noise and is intended to absorb that. The decode axis is not
under test in this experiment and I make no claim on it; the change is confined
to a kernel that the decode path reaches only through the seed prefill.

## 7. Learning carried forward

The single most useful thing established here is the seed-prefill identity in
§1. It changes the price of every prefill-side optimization in this campaign by
a factor of about 1.47, and it explains a class of confusing past results where
a purely prefill-side change appeared to move the decode number. Any future
reader differencing these two receipts should apply it before interpreting
either axis.
